metaDescription: Six vertical computer mice compared by tilt angle, hand fit, connections, noise and DPI, to help you choose a handshake-style mouse that suits your desk.
introParagraphs: A vertical mouse stands your hand up on its edge, so the palm faces inward the way it would in a handshake instead of facing the desk. The idea is simple, but the execution varies: some tilt at about 57 degrees, some at 58, some are sized for small hands and others for medium ones, and the connection options range from a single USB receiver to Bluetooth plus a receiver on three devices.

This guide compares six vertical mice. The Logitech MX Vertical is the premium, ergonomist-tested choice. The Logitech Lift is the smaller, softer sibling. The ProtoArc EM11 NL is the compact rechargeable option. The UGREEN is the quiet one, the TECKNET is the many-DPI-levels one, and the Anker is the simplest. All of them are right-hand designs, which is worth stating up front. Tilt angles are stated only on the Logitech and ProtoArc listings, so we say so wherever the others leave it out.

We evaluated each from listing specifications and buyer feedback patterns, not from hands-on bench work, and we judged them on fit, ease of switching from a flat mouse, and day-to-day convenience. A few days of adjustment is normal with any vertical mouse. If you have ongoing hand or wrist discomfort, a doctor or occupational therapist can advise better than any buying guide.

products.name: Logitech MX Vertical Wireless Mouse

specList.label: Testing
specList.value: Designed with ergonomist criteria per listing

products.description:
The MX Vertical is the benchmark that other vertical mice are measured against. The listing describes a natural handshake position, a unique 57 degree angle, and a design tested against criteria set by ergonomists, along with the ability to move content between three computers. The thumb is supported rather than stretched, which is a big part of why the shape feels natural.

The tradeoff is price tier and size. It is the most expensive mouse in the guide, and the body is larger than the Lift, so people with small hands may prefer the Lift or the ProtoArc. Like every vertical mouse, it takes several days of use before pointing feels automatic.

Compared with the Lift, the MX Vertical suits medium to large hands and has the more elaborate feature set. Compared with the budget models, it has the best-documented design process. If you spend most of your day at a computer and want a vertical mouse with proven credentials, this is the one to start with. Setup is simple: pair it over Bluetooth, move content between three computers, and spend your first week on easy tasks so the new posture settles in. It sits on a plain desk or pad without fuss, and the wide body is easy to find by feel, which helps if you work with the lights low.
products.bestFor: Medium to large right hands and heavy daily computer use.
cons: Larger body, less ideal for small hands

products.badge: Best for Small to Medium Hands
products.name: Logitech Lift Vertical Ergonomic Wireless Mouse
products.description:
Lift shares the MX Vertical's 57 degree angle but shrinks the body for smaller hands. The listing says it is a great fit for small to medium hands, and that the softly textured grip and snug thumb rest let you rest the hand upright through the day. It connects over Bluetooth or the included Logi Bolt receiver, and comes in graphite or rose.

The tradeoff is that large hands will feel it is undersized, and the feature set is simpler than the MX Vertical. It does not move content between computers in the way the premium model does. It is right-handed only, and the soft grip can pick up dust over time.

Compared with the ProtoArc EM11 NL, the Lift is from a better-known brand and sits higher in the price tier. Compared with the MX Vertical, it is smaller and lighter. If you want a polished vertical mouse in a size that fits most women and many men with smaller hands, it is the safe choice. Setup takes only a minute, and the upright shape is easy to settle into once you stop gripping tightly. Keep it on a clean pad, and wipe the soft grip occasionally, because lighter colors like rose show marks more than graphite does.
products.bestFor: Small to medium hands that want a polished, mainstream vertical mouse.

products.name: ProtoArc EM11 NL Wireless Vertical Mouse
products.description:
The EM11 NL has the steepest tilt in the group, 58 degrees, and a fit statement that is unusually specific: hand lengths under 7.5 inches. The listing adds a built-in 500mAh lithium-ion battery that charges by cable, and connections for up to three devices through dual Bluetooth and a 2.4G USB-A receiver.

The tradeoff is that it is deliberately small, so anyone with a longer hand should look at the MX Vertical instead. A rechargeable battery means you must remember to plug it in, and the listing does not state a runtime in the text we have. The brand is less familiar than Logitech.

Compared with the Lift, it adds a rechargeable battery and three-device support at a lower price tier. Compared with the UGREEN, it is more specific about who it fits. For a smaller hand and a laptop plus tablet setup, it is thoughtful value. Plug in the cable to charge before first use, then pair it with your main device and keep the receiver in a port for the second. If you carry it in a bag, the upright body is bulkier than a flat travel mouse, so give it a pocket of its own.
products.bestFor: Smaller hands and multi-device desks that prefer charging to batteries.

products.name: UGREEN Ergonomic Wireless Vertical Mouse
products.description:
UGREEN is the vertical mouse for people who share a room. The listing describes quiet-click buttons, a five-button layout and four DPI levels (1000, 1600, 2000 and 4000), along with Bluetooth and 2.4G connections for up to three devices. The shape follows a natural vertical handshake position.

The tradeoff is documentation. The listing does not give an exact tilt angle or dimensions in the text we have, so fit is something to judge from photos. It also lacks the brand support of Logitech. The low price tier is its strength.

Compared with the TECKNET, it has fewer DPI steps but clearer quiet-click messaging. Compared with the Anker, it adds Bluetooth. If you want a low-cost vertical mouse that will not click loudly in a bedroom or office, start here. Because the clicks are subdued, you can use it in a quiet kitchen or study, and the five buttons let you step through browser pages without reaching for the keyboard. Treat the dpi button as a set-and-forget control once you have found a speed you like.
products.bestFor: Quiet rooms and shared offices on a modest budget.

products.name: TECKNET Wireless Bluetooth Vertical Mouse 4800 DPI
products.description:
The TECKNET vertical mouse is the specs-heavy option. The listing gives six DPI levels up to 4800, Bluetooth 5.0 and 3.0 plus a 2.4GHz USB-A receiver, three-device switching and a quiet operation that the maker says suits libraries. The vertical shape supports a handshake posture.

The tradeoff is that high DPI helps mostly on big monitors, and the many levels may be more than a casual user wants. The listing does not state a tilt angle or battery runtime in the text we have. It is right-handed.

Compared with the UGREEN, it has more DPI steps and a higher ceiling. Compared with the MX Vertical, it is far less documented but far cheaper. For a user with a large display and multiple devices, it is a flexible budget pick. It suits a desk with a big screen, where the higher dpi steps let you cross the display with a small wrist movement. Pick one speed for daily use and avoid the temptation to keep changing it, as that makes the pointer feel unpredictable.
products.bestFor: Large monitors and multi-device desks on a budget.

products.name: Anker 2.4G Wireless Vertical Ergonomic Mouse
products.description:
Anker keeps vertical mice simple. The listing describes a scientifically designed ergonomic shape, optical tracking at 800, 1200 and 1600 DPI, and next and previous buttons for web browsing. It connects through a 2.4G USB receiver, so there is no pairing to do.

The tradeoff is flexibility. A receiver needs a USB-A port, there is no Bluetooth, and the DPI range is modest. The listing does not state a tilt angle in the text we have.

Compared with the UGREEN and TECKNET, it is simpler and less feature-rich. Compared with the Lift, it is cheaper and plainer. If you want to test the vertical idea without spending much, the Anker is the low-risk way in. It needs no software and no pairing, which makes it a calm choice for a shared family computer. Keep the receiver in a rear port so it is not knocked out, and remember that a battery change is the only maintenance it will ever need.
products.bestFor: Testing a vertical mouse with the least fuss.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The tilt decides how far the forearm rotates. The MX Vertical and the Lift use 57 degrees, and the ProtoArc EM11 NL uses 58. A steeper angle turns the hand closer to a pure handshake. Listings without an angle, such as UGREEN, TECKNET and Anker, leave you to judge from photos. The steeper the tilt, the more your wrist turns, so a first-time user should treat 57 degrees as a good starting point, not a rule.

Vertical mice are less forgiving of poor fit than flat ones, because the hand rests on the side. The Lift suits small to medium hands, the EM11 NL suits hands under 7.5 inches and the MX Vertical suits larger ones. A mouse that is too small makes the fingers curl. Measure your hand before ordering. Check also the shape of the base, because a wide base keeps the little finger from dragging on the desk.

In a vertical mouse the thumb carries more of the work. The Lift has a snug thumb rest, the MX Vertical has a supported thumb position, and others rely on the body shape. A good thumb rest keeps the thumb from stretching. Look for a visible, contoured thumb area. If you hold the thumb in a stretched position for hours, the benefit of the vertical shape fades, so look for support under the thumb.

The EM11 NL, UGREEN, TECKNET and Uineer-style models connect three devices through Bluetooth and a receiver. The Lift offers Bluetooth or Logi Bolt, and the Anker offers only a receiver. Choose multi-device if you swap computers. Choose a receiver if you want zero setup. Bluetooth pairing varies by system, so read the quick-start card once and keep it with the box.

Vertical mice sit upright, which can make clicks echo. UGREEN highlights quiet clicks and TECKNET silent operation. In shared spaces, this matters more than a few extra DPI levels. Try the clicks if you can. A quiet mouse also helps video calls, because the microphone does not pick up each click.

Expect a few days of clumsy pointing. Start with browsing and email, then move to tasks needing precision. If a mouse still feels wrong after two weeks, return it. The right size makes the adjustment easier. Keep the old mouse close in the first week so you can switch back for a precision task without frustration.

howWeEvaluated.title: Angle and posture
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated angles: 57 degrees on the MX Vertical and the Lift, 58 on the EM11 NL. Listings with no angle were rated more cautiously. A stated number is more useful than the word ergonomic, which every vertical mouse uses.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We read size statements, from the Lift's small to medium to the EM11 NL's hands under 7.5 inches and the MX Vertical's larger body. We treated a size statement as the strongest sign that a maker had tested the shape on real hands.

howWeEvaluated.title: Connection
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared Bluetooth, receiver and multi-device options across the six mice, noting the Anker's receiver only approach. Mice that pair with three devices were rated above those that pair with one for households with several computers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Daily comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at thumb support, grips and click noise, with extra credit for the Lift's soft grip and the UGREEN's quiet buttons. Soft materials and a clear thumb rest earned credit because the thumb works harder in this shape.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The MX Vertical leads on documented design, the Lift on polish, EM11 NL on small-hand fit, UGREEN on quiet, TECKNET on DPI and Anker on simplicity. The MX Vertical became our overall pick. The ranking weights fit and documentation first, extras second, and price tier last.

faq.q: Is a vertical mouse hard to learn?
faq.a: It takes a few days for most people. Pointing and clicking feel unfamiliar at first because the wrist is no longer flat, and the first afternoon often feels clumsy. Start with browsing and email, then move on to tasks that need precision, and give it at least a week before deciding.

faq.q: Do vertical mice come in left-hand versions?
faq.a: Most of the mice in this guide are right-hand designs, because the thumb rest and buttons are shaped for the right side. Check the listing before buying, and look for a dedicated left-hand model if you need one. Left-handers who cannot find one may be more comfortable with a symmetrical standard mouse.

There is no single best angle. The MX Vertical and Lift use 57 degrees and the EM11 NL uses 58, so the difference is tiny. Comfort depends far more on hand size and how well the body fits than on a degree or two.

faq.q: Are cheap vertical mice any good?
faq.a: Many are fine for light use and they let you test the idea for little money. They usually offer less documentation, fewer software options and weaker support than Logitech. Use the return window to check fit, and do not judge the whole category by one poor sample.

faq.q: Will it work with a tablet?
faq.a: Bluetooth models such as the Lift, EM11 NL, UGREEN and TECKNET can pair with tablets that accept a mouse. The Anker uses a USB-A receiver, so it needs an adapter or a computer. Check your tablet's mouse support before buying.

faq.q: Can a mouse replace medical advice?
faq.a: No. A vertical mouse is a comfort choice, not a treatment. If you have lasting discomfort in the hand, wrist or forearm, ask a doctor or occupational therapist for guidance, and consider desk height and chair setup too.

faq.q: How do I clean a vertical mouse?
faq.a: Wipe the body with a slightly damp cloth, never soaking it, and clean the sensor window with a dry cotton swab. Soft grip coatings on models like the Lift collect dust, so a quick wipe each week keeps them looking fresh. Avoid harsh cleaners, which can dull the surface.
